title: VLM and LLM GPU memory usage grows across repeated requests until OOM
body: When I send repeated image requests to an SGLang server hosting a VLM, GPU memory usage continuously increases until an OOM occurs. I have also observed growth with several text and multimodal configurations, although text-only gpt-oss did not show it. VLMs reach OOM more often because they have a larger footprint, including the ViT, activations, and sometimes a fast image processor. Version 0.4.9.post6 has a severe VLM memory leak when the fast image processor is used and should be avoided. I published the reproduction setup and memory plots for gpt-oss, Llama 3.2, Qwen2.5, Qwen2.5-VL, and InternVL3.

symptoms_visible: When I repeatedly send image requests to an SGLang VLM server, GPU memory usage keeps increasing until the server runs out of memory.
I also see increasing memory in several text and multimodal configurations, while text-only gpt-oss remains stable.
Qwen2.5-VL sometimes shows sudden memory surges in addition to the gradual increase.
N0.label: N0 repeated-request VRAM growth reported

symptoms_visible: Qwen2.5-3B memory still rises over time when radix cache is enabled.
Using a lower static-memory fraction shifts the entire memory curve downward, but the rising shape remains.
N1.label: N1 cache and static-memory controls tested

symptoms_visible: Under sequential Qwen2.5-VL requests with cache flushing every 50 requests and CUDA graph and radix cache disabled, the memory plots differ with and without image processing, but memory growth remains observable.
N2.label: N2 image-processing contribution compared

symptoms_visible: After switching to 0.4.10.post2, GPU memory still grows on Qwen2.5-VL and the workload can still end in OOM or a server restart.
N2_x.label: N2_x version downgrade aftermath

symptoms_visible: With the proposed patch, VRAM no longer keeps growing during my VLM workload.
After the multimodal workload finishes, the spawned Python process can remain present in memory.
N3.label: N3 candidate memory fix verified

symptoms_visible: The proposed patch stops the continuing VRAM growth that was still present on 0.4.10.post2.
The spawned Python process can remain present after the multimodal workload completes.
N3_x.label: N3_x candidate fix verified after downgrade failed

symptoms_visible: On a current build containing the memory-usage fix, repeated VLM requests no longer cause VRAM consumption to grow continuously toward OOM.
N_terminal.label: terminal original VRAM-growth issue resolved

question_patterns: Does the same growth occur on a text model when radix cache is enabled?
Can you repeat the text-model workload without disabling radix cache and share the memory curve?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I repeated it with Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B and radix cache enabled. The plot title is wrong, but the memory curve still rises in a very similar way.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: With radix cache enabled, the memory curve stays completely flat for the same Qwen text workload.
The curve grows at a slightly different rate, but it still rises with radix cache enabled.

question_patterns: How does changing the static-memory fraction affect the curve?
Can you repeat the workload with a lower mem-fraction-static value?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Reducing --mem-fraction-static shifts the curve to a lower memory level, while its overall rising shape remains.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Reducing the static-memory fraction makes the curve flat and prevents any further increase.

question_patterns: Can you compare the same VLM workload with and without initializing image processing?
Please run matched VLM tests with and without image processing and share both memory curves.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I compared Qwen2.5-VL with image processing on the right and without it on the left. Both runs used sequential requests, flush_cache every 50 requests, --disable-cuda-graph, and --disable-radix-cache. Here is the side-by-side memory plot.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The no-image-processing run is completely stable, while only the image-processing run grows until OOM.
The two runs have slightly different peaks, but both still show increasing memory.

solution.intent: Avoid the current leak by switching the deployment to SGLang 0.4.10.post2, which was reported as trustworthy.
solution.concrete_example: Install sglang[all]==0.4.10.post2 and rerun the same VLM workload.

edges.comment: From c20-c22 and c17: 0.4.10.post2 was recommended as trustworthy, but other affected inference users reproduced GPU-memory growth and OOM/server restart on that version, including Qwen2.5-VL. Their systems are folded into the affected user side.

question_patterns: Can you check whether the same VLM workload is stable on the suggested older build?
Please run the reproduction against 0.4.10.post2 and report whether memory remains stable.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tested 0.4.10.post2 with Qwen2.5-VL, and it also has GPU memory growth. In another run the workload failed after a couple of minutes and the server restarted.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The same long-running VLM workload remains flat and completes without OOM on 0.4.10.post2.

question_patterns: Can you test the proposed patch with your usual multimodal workload and monitor VRAM growth?
Please run the candidate branch under the same VLM load and report whether memory continues increasing.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tested the proposed patch, and it effectively resolved the VRAM consumption growth issue with my VLM workload. After the multimodal workload completes, the spawned Python process still remains hanging in memory.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The candidate branch still shows the same continuous VRAM growth and reaches OOM.
The candidate branch has a slightly different peak, but VRAM remains bounded and the workload completes.

solution.intent: Use a current SGLang build containing the accepted peak-memory reduction fix, then verify under the original repeated VLM workload that VRAM remains bounded instead of growing toward OOM.
solution.concrete_example: Update from an affected release to a current source build containing the accepted memory-usage patch, rerun the same image-request workload, and monitor allocated and reserved GPU memory over time before declaring the issue resolved.
solution.inference_hint: The thread does not describe the linked patch's internal implementation, so the diagnosis should remain at the demonstrated level: repeated request processing causes unbounded non-static GPU-memory growth, image processing can add pressure, and the accepted patch bounds peak VRAM. Do not invent a more specific code-level mechanism.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the established failure mode without inventing an unsupported code-level cause: repeated VLM and some LLM requests grow non-static GPU memory until OOM, with multimodal image processing adding memory pressure.

Diagnosis must be grounded in the collected controls: growth also occurs with radix cache enabled, lowering static allocation shifts the baseline without removing the rising trend, and matched VLM runs compare operation with and without image processing.
Must recommend using a current build containing the accepted peak-memory reduction fix and verifying that VRAM remains bounded under the original repeated-request workload.
Must not present 0.4.10.post2 as a reliable fix; affected users reproduced GPU-memory growth and OOM on that version.
Must not conflate the separate post-workload lingering Python process with failure of the original continuous-VRAM-growth fix.
Must treat the original OOM issue as resolved only after an affected user verifies the fixed build; the reporter's final confirmation supplies that terminal evidence.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical ML systems engineer who can launch many model configurations, control SGLang cache and CUDA settings, monitor GPU-memory curves, compare workloads, and test source builds. Multiple affected inference operators are folded into the simulated user side.
persona_hint.communication_style: Experiment-driven and concise; shares exact launch flags and plots, distinguishes observations from tentative guesses, and readily runs controlled comparisons or candidate patches.
